solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Kind of wood panelling originally inside directly opposite

indicators.note: what comes originally comes at the start, so only the opening letter of the word is wanted
a thing placed inside another sits within it, so one piece goes into the middle of the other

blocks.note: polar opposites are as far apart as it is possible to be
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A carpenter describing the wood of some panelling that sits opposite.
explanation.walkthrough: P is slipped into POLAR, giving PO-P-LAR. 'Kind of wood' reads as part of the panelling description but is the whole definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Poplar is a tree whose pale, soft timber is used for furniture and plywood, so it names a type of wood.

clue.text: Delay appointment only after pressure

blocks.note: a post is a job or position someone is appointed to
P is the standard symbol for pressure in physics
'the only one' sense: a single one

explanation.surface: Someone pushing back a meeting, but only once the pressure is on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appointment' wants to be a meeting, which suits 'Delay'; here it is a job someone is appointed to. P is the physics symbol for pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: To postpone is to put an event off until a later time, the same as delaying it.

clue.text: Make impossible claims primarily during introduction

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so just the leading letter of the word is used
something happening during another event falls within its span, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: a prelude is an opening piece that introduces what follows
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A speaker making far-fetched claims right at the start of their introduction.
explanation.walkthrough: C goes inside PRELUDE. 'Make impossible claims' looks like one phrase about boasting, but the definition stops after 'impossible'.
explanation.definitionFit: To preclude something is to rule it out in advance, preventing it from happening at all.

clue.text: Still finding theatre staff accommodating

indicators.note: to accommodate is to give room to, so the run of letters is housed within the phrase

blocks.note: the letters run across the join between the two words

explanation.surface: Theatre staff housing someone, perhaps a touring actor.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits across 'theATRE STaff'. 'Still' looks like an adverb meaning 'even now' but is an adjective meaning motionless.
explanation.definitionFit: Something motionless is described as being at rest, an idiom for not moving at all.

clue.text: A bit of support with money mostly to get gin

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: brass is slang for money, cut short by one letter
a gin is an old word for a snare used to catch animals

explanation.surface: Someone wanting a little financial backing so they can buy a bottle of gin.
explanation.walkthrough: BRASS is British slang for money; dropping its last S leaves BRAS. 'Gin' wants to be the drink, but it is the trap (as in gin trap).
explanation.definitionFit: A bra strap is one small part of a brassiere, the garment worn for support, so it is literally a bit of support.

clue.text: Unusual attention on the rise stifling resistance

indicators.note: in a down entry something on the rise reads upward, so the letters run from bottom to top
to stifle is to smother, wrapping around something so it is held inside

blocks.note: to have someone's ear is to have their attention
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: Unusual levels of interest are growing and suppressing any opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: EAR turned upward gives RAE, then R goes inside: RA-R-E.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rare is seldom found or seen, which is what being unusual means.

clue.text: The only one to assume provocative artist is Native American

indicators.note: to assume is to take on, as one takes on a garment, so one piece takes the other into itself

blocks.note: the sole one is the only one there is
Tracey Emin, the British artist known for provocative works such as her unmade bed

explanation.surface: A claim that the only shocking artist around is of Native American heritage.
explanation.walkthrough: Tracey Emin is a British artist famous for confrontational work such as her unmade bed, which is why she is 'provocative'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Seminole are a Native American people originally from Florida, so the name is an example of the category.

clue.text: Highly unpleasant when leaked by police

blocks.note: colours or liquids that leak are said to have run
the Criminal Investigation Department, the British detective branch

explanation.surface: Something becoming very nasty once the police leak it to the press.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaked by police' suggests a news story, but 'leaked' is what running colours do and 'by' means next to. The CID is the British police's detective branch.
explanation.definitionFit: Rancid describes food, especially fat or butter, gone off and foul-smelling, so it is strongly disagreeable.

clue.text: Dog perhaps taking in completely straw-filled bed

indicators.note: taking something in means admitting it within, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a dog is one example of a household pet
all the way, all in: entirely

explanation.surface: A dog curling up entirely in a bed of straw.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog perhaps' is a definition by example, so it leads to the general word PET, which then surrounds ALL.
explanation.definitionFit: A pallet is a crude mattress stuffed with straw, or a makeshift bed laid on the floor.

clue.text: Vows to accept damage over time on board

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece is received inside another

blocks.note: wear is the gradual damage that comes from use over time
aboard ship is conventionally shown by S...S, the steamship abbreviation

explanation.surface: Promises made to put up with long-term damage on a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On board' signals the letters SS, the steamship abbreviation, going around WEAR. 'Over time' belongs with 'damage', not the time letter T.
explanation.definitionFit: To swear is to make a solemn promise, so as a verb it means the same as vows.

clue.text: A short time after, the king meets international gangster? Deplorable

indicators.note: one thing coming after another follows it, so the earlier words are placed second in the answer

blocks.note: Carolus Rex, Latin for King Charles
I is a standard abbreviation for international
a minute, shortened to its abbreviation
Al Capone, the Chicago gangster

explanation.surface: Moments after the monarch meets a mobster, a shocked commentator calls it disgraceful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gangster' looks like the definition but is Al Capone; the definition is 'Deplorable'. CR stands for Carolus Rex, Latin for King Charles.
explanation.definitionFit: Criminal is used informally to mean shameful or disgraceful, as in 'a criminal waste'.

clue.text: Insincere FBI agent obtaining predominating influence after Hoover finally leaves

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the closing letter of the name is picked out
something that leaves is no longer there, so a letter is taken away
obtaining means getting hold of, so one piece holds the other within it

blocks.note: a Fed is American slang for a federal agent
a reign is a period of dominant rule or influence
the final letter of the name, removed from the influence word

explanation.surface: An FBI man fakes his loyalty while grabbing power once J Edgar Hoover departs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hoover' looks like J Edgar Hoover, the long-serving FBI director, which fits the surface perfectly, but only his last letter matters. A Fed is American slang for a federal agent.
explanation.definitionFit: Feigned means pretended or put on, describing feelings that are not genuine.

clue.text: An architectural feature most unlikely to be found in bridge support

indicators.note: something found in another sits within it, so one piece lies inside the other

blocks.note: a pier is a pillar holding up a span of a bridge
as in 'the last person you would expect': the least likely

explanation.surface: A feature of architecture you would never expect to find in a bridge's supports.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Most unlikely' reads as a comment on the surface, as in 'the last place you would look', but supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilaster is a flat rectangular column projecting slightly from a wall, a decorative architectural element.

clue.text: Is Enid somehow positioned to obtain exclusive information?

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters can be arranged any way that works

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Asking whether Enid has somehow got herself placed to get a scoop.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a long phrase rather than a single word, and the question mark flags its playful looseness.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the inside of an organisation means being placed where privileged, secret knowledge is available.

clue.text: Turn violently when caught about to join revolutionary uprising

indicators.note: in a down entry an uprising goes upward, so the word reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
on as in 'a book on birds': concerning
a Trot is a Trotskyist, a revolutionary

explanation.surface: Someone captured just before joining a rebel uprising twists about wildly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary uprising' looks like one noun phrase, but 'uprising' turns the revolutionary over. Trot is short for Trotskyist.
explanation.definitionFit: To contort is to twist something forcibly out of its normal shape, a violent kind of twisting.

clue.text: Tennis star ultimately departing with nothing

indicators.note: the ultimate part is the very end, and departing means going, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: Rafael Nadal, the Spanish tennis champion

explanation.surface: A tennis player finally leaving the tournament empty-handed.
explanation.walkthrough: NADAL loses his last letter. Fittingly, nada is Spanish, like Nadal.
explanation.definitionFit: Nada is a Spanish word for zero, borrowed into English slang for not a thing at all.

clue.text: Mean to get money once soldier returns to the front

indicators.note: returning means coming back the way one went, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: a GI is an American soldier
a noble was an old English gold coin

explanation.surface: Someone planning to cash in once a soldier comes back from the front line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To the front' looks like the battle front but just puts IG at the start. A noble was a medieval English gold coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Mean in the sense of base or contemptible matches ignoble, meaning dishonourable and lacking principle.

clue.text: Stadium announcer’s aid Bale smashed following a friendly!

indicators.note: something smashed is broken into bits, so these letters are reassembled differently

blocks.note: taken as written
a microphone, which an announcer speaks into
taken as written; Gareth Bale is a Welsh footballer

explanation.surface: A stadium announcer hailing Gareth Bale's thumping shot in a friendly match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following a' puts the rest after A. 'Friendly' looks like a friendly match, the football setting of the surface, but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Amicable describes relations that are good-natured and free of hostility, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Some die tragically after hospital trotters in Bolton

indicators.note: a tragic turn wrecks things, so the letters come out wrecked into a new order

blocks.note: H is the map and sign abbreviation for hospital
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grim tale of deaths after a hospital stay, with pigs' feet somewhere in Bolton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trotters' looks like pigs' feet, but Bolton Wanderers, an English football club, are nicknamed the Trotters, so at their ground they are the home side.
explanation.definitionFit: Playing in Bolton, the club nicknamed the Trotters is the host team rather than the visitors.

clue.text: Lasting ill-will enveloping fellow Irish chap with fierce temper

indicators.note: to envelop is to wrap all round, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: spite is persistent malice towards someone
F is the abbreviation for fellow
IR is a standard abbreviation for Irish

explanation.surface: A grudge-bearing Irishman with a short fuse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Irish chap' reads as one person, but 'Irish' belongs to the wordplay and 'chap' to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A spitfire is a person, often thought of as hot-headed, who flares up quickly in anger.

clue.text: General pardon from Trump at the outset welcomed by worried yes-man

indicators.note: the outset is the beginning, so only the opening letter of the name is taken
worried in the sense of tugged and fretted at, so the letters are pulled out of order
a guest welcomed by a host is taken in, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: the opening letter of the name
taken as written, without the hyphen

explanation.surface: A nervous sycophant greeting a sweeping pardon issued by Trump.
explanation.walkthrough: The YESMAN letters are rearranged as AMNESY and T goes inside. 'General' looks like a military rank but means 'broad', applying to the pardon.
explanation.definitionFit: An amnesty is an official pardon granted to a whole class of offenders, hence general rather than individual.

clue.text: Nothing in fool’s flattery

indicators.note: one thing in another is held within it, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: a sap is a gullible, foolish person
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Flattery from a fool contains nothing of substance.
explanation.walkthrough: O goes inside SAP; the 's after 'fool' is read as 'is', joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft soap is an idiom for smooth persuasive praise, and soap alone can mean the same flattery.

clue.text: Indication of agreement raised in support of Chinese delegate

indicators.note: in a down entry raising something lifts it upward, so its letters read bottom to top
in a down entry a support sits underneath, so one piece comes below the other

blocks.note: the Han are China's majority ethnic group
a nod of the head signals yes

explanation.surface: A show of hands raised to back a delegate from China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delegate' looks like a noun, a conference representative, but it is the verb: to pass a task to someone else.
explanation.definitionFit: To delegate a job is to pass it along to another person, which is what handing it on means.

clue.text: Stock car eventually owned by Mark

indicators.note: eventually means in the end, so only the final letter of the word is used
what is owned is held by its owner, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: a stain is a mark left on a surface
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A stock car that ends up belonging to a man called Mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stock car' reads as one motor-racing term, but 'Stock' alone is the definition. 'Mark' looks like a name and is just a blemish.
explanation.definitionFit: Stock and strain both mean a line of descent or breed, as of animals or plants.

clue.text: That’s extremely risky near large patch of willows

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outermost letters are kept

blocks.note: OS is the clothing abbreviation for outsize
i.e., Latin id est, means 'that is'
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: A warning that it is very dangerous to go near a big clump of willow trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's' looks like a throat-clearing opener but is the abbreviation i.e., Latin for 'that is'. Outsize is the clothing size for large.
explanation.definitionFit: Osiers are a kind of willow grown for basket-making, and an osiery is the plantation where they grow.

clue.text: Criticise volunteers upset by change of course

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over, so in an across entry its letters end up back to front

blocks.note: the Territorial Army, Britain's former volunteer reserve force
to tack is to change a sailing boat's direction

explanation.surface: Volunteers annoyed by a sudden switch in plans start complaining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like 'annoyed' in the surface, but it turns TA over. The TA was Britain's Territorial Army, part-time volunteer soldiers.
explanation.definitionFit: To attack someone verbally is to criticise them harshly, the figurative sense of an assault.

clue.text: Scene showing plaintiff at first overwhelmed by dull discourse at court

indicators.note: what comes at first is at the start, so just the opening letter is used
to be overwhelmed is to be engulfed, so one piece is swallowed inside the other

blocks.note: prose is plain, ordinary writing or speech, as in 'prosaic'
the opening letter of the word
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A courtroom scene where the plaintiff is buried under tedious legal argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scene' looks like the courtroom drama of the surface but means a view over a landscape.
explanation.definitionFit: A prospect is an extensive view of a landscape, the same sense as a scene laid out before one.

clue.text: Permit to go through

blocks.note: first meaning: a document granting permission to enter
second meaning: to move past or across something

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one phrase, a permit allowing entry, but splits into two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A pass is a written authorisation, and to pass is to travel through or beyond a place.

clue.text: Fear missing runs with batter exhausted

indicators.note: missing means lacking, so a letter is taken away from the word

blocks.note: dread is deep fear
R is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for runs, removed here
to batter someone is to beat them

explanation.surface: A worn-out cricket batter, scared of failing to score.
explanation.walkthrough: DREAD drops R to give DEAD. 'Runs' and 'batter' both suggest cricket, but 'batter' is a verb: to beat.
explanation.definitionFit: Dead beat is an informal British phrase for utterly tired, completely worn out.

clue.text: Doctor on island of a once powerful Italian family

blocks.note: a general informal word for a physician or army medical orderly
I is the map abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A doctor stationed on an island owned by an old Italian dynasty.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' simply places one piece before the other.
explanation.definitionFit: The Medici were the banking dynasty that ruled Florence during the Renaissance, a once dominant Italian family.

clue.text: Bull’s balls

blocks.note: first meaning: short for a coarse slang word for rubbish talk
second meaning: slang for foolish talk or rubbish

explanation.walkthrough: The possessive suggests a bull's testicles, but the 's means 'is', linking two slang words for the same thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Both bull and balls are informal slang terms for talk that is foolish, untrue or meaningless.

clue.text: Somewhat racy beleaguered Phrygian goddess

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only part of the run of letters is wanted

blocks.note: the letters span the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A rather risqué goddess from ancient Phrygia under siege.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs through 'raCY BELEaguered'. Phrygia was an ancient kingdom in what is now Turkey.
explanation.definitionFit: Cybele was the great mother goddess worshipped in Phrygia, later adopted by Greece and Rome.
